questions.prompt: In the BFS code, what does `if (visited.Add(next))` achieve?
options: It sorts the neighbours before they are enqueued
It removes the node from the graph once visited
It enqueues a node only the first time it is seen, because `Add` returns `false` if it is already present
It throws if the graph contains a cycle
questions.explanation: `HashSet<T>.Add` returns `false` for a value already in the set, so the same check both marks the node visited and stops it being enqueued twice.

questions.prompt: You need the shortest path in an unweighted grid. Which search does the lesson pick?
questions.explanation: BFS explores level by level with a `Queue<T>`, so the first time it reaches the target is along a shortest path in an unweighted graph.

questions.prompt: The graph is very deep and recursive DFS risks a stack overflow. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Use a `HashSet<T>` instead of a graph
Increase the recursion depth with a larger `visited` set
Use BFS or an iterative DFS
questions.explanation: The quick-pick table lists BFS or iterative DFS (with an explicit `Stack<T>`) for very deep graphs, and DFS for very wide graphs where a BFS queue would be memory heavy.

questions.prompt: Hash-based search is O(1) on average. Which of these is one of its drawbacks?
options: It needs the input to be sorted
It cannot answer ordering or range queries such as "next greater" or "between a and b"
It is O(log n) per lookup
It only works on integer keys
questions.explanation: Hashing jumps straight to a bucket, so it keeps no order: no range queries. It also uses extra memory, relies on correct `Equals`/`GetHashCode`, and can hit O(n) with heavy collisions.
